Preference and Taste
---
Different people give different answers. 
In economics, we make no attempt to explain why people prefer the things they do. 
Instead, we take those preferences as given and try to figure out how they govern behavior.

Preference and Taste
---
Which do you prefer: eggs or root beer? 
Actually, that’s a bad question—for several reasons. 
First, your answer might depend on the quantities involved. 
Second, the answer might depend on how many eggs and how much root beer you’ve already got. 
Is this a question about which of the two you’d least want to forgo forever, or a question about which you’d like to receive for your birthday?

The Composite-Good Convention
---
In order to draw indifference curve diagrams, we must assume that there are only two goods in the world. 
Seems restricting, yet in fact it is not.

The Composite-Good Convention
---
In many applications we will want to concentrate our attention on a single good—say, eggs.
In that case we divide the world into two classes of goods, namely, “eggs” and “things that are not eggs,” otherwise known as “all other goods.” 
This allows us to draw indifference curves between eggs (on the horizontal axis) and all other goods (on the vertical).

The Composite-Good Convention
---
There remains the problem of units. 
What is a single unit of all other goods?
The simplest solution to this problem is to measure all other goods in terms of their dollar value.
When we lump together all things that are not eggs and measure it in a single unit like dollars, we say that we are using the composite-good convention.

The Composite-Good Convention
---
In the presence of the composite-good convention, the slope of an indifference curve is the marginal value of an egg in terms of other goods, with the other goods measured in dollars. 
Thus, it is the minimum number of dollars for which the consumer would be willing to trade an egg.
The budget constraint

How Much Money You Have to Spend
---
The budget set is the set of all possible bundles of goods and services that a consumer can purchase with her income. 
Economists usually describe the budget set in the context of another concept—the budget constraint.

budget constraint
---
First, we’ll assume that consumers do not save or borrow. 
Second, we plot the budget constraint as a smooth line, even though our examples will be using whole units.

First, we’ll assume that consumers do not save or borrow. We know,

Application #1Price Indices

Price Indices
---
To measure how people are affected by price changes, government statistical department around the world often report price indices
Chinese statistics department publishes what is known as the CPI (consumer price index)

Price Indices
---
Roughly, statistics department do this by tracking the cost of a given basket (a fixed bundle of goods and services) over time. 
If the basket gets more expensive, they say that the cost of living has gone up (which  may imply that people are worse off)
If the basket gets cheaper, they say that the cost of living has gone down (which may imply that people are better off).

Price Indices
---
Example: 
Harold consumes goods X and Y. 
Their initial prices are 3 and 4, respectively
With an income of 20, he (optimally) chooses to buy 4 units of X and 2 of Y.
Now the price of X rises to 4 while the price of Y falls to 2
Suppose his income remains at 20 dollars. ?  Has his living standard change? If yes, is he better or worse off than before?

Price Indices
---
Suppose we choose the following basket as a benchmark and hold the basket fixed: 4 units of X and 2 units of Y.
The original cost of the basket: 20
The new cost of the same basket: still 20
So the price index does not change
Question: does Harold feel the same as before?

slides.notes:
Look again. Basket O costs $20 under the original prices and still $20 under the new prices. If you track basket O,
you’ll say the cost of living hasn’t changed at all. That can be misleading, because, as we’ve just seen, Harold is definitely happier with the new prices than with the old ones.

If you tracked basket P, you’d get a different answer. Basket P is outside the Original budget line, which means it must cost more than $20 at the original prices. But it is exactly on the New budget line, so it costs just $20 at the new prices. So if you used P to measure the cost of living you’d say that the cost of living had come down.

slides.text:
Price Indices
---
The problem:
With this approach, you are using a fixed basket, but the answer you get depends on which basket you choose to track.

Laspeyres v.s. Paasche price index
---
The cost-of-living measurement that you get by tracking the original is called a Laspeyres price index , it tends to make things look worse than they are. 
The cost-of-living measurement that you get by tracking the new basket (in this case P) is called a Paasche price index , it tends to make things look better than they are. 
Unfortunately, there is no perfect way to measure changes in the cost of living. Sometimes people use Fisher index
Application #2Differences in taste?

Difference in taste?
---
Economists don’t like to attribute differences in patterns of human behavior across countries, cultures, groups people to taste differences across countries, cultures, etc. 
They normally think of the difference in behavior as a result of people facing different constraints. 
So are there wide-ranged differences in taste?
Difference in taste
slides.notes:
Albert buys tomatoes for $4 each and potatoes for $3 each. His income is $60 per day.
Betty buys tomatoes for $2 each and potatoes for $4 each. Her income is $48 per day.
Now we are told that Albert chooses the basket (12, 4). We check that Betty can more than afford this point, so it must be inside her budget line, on the boldfaced part of Albert’s line. 
We plot that point, and the corresponding tangency, in the second panel, where it is labeled A. We are also told that Betty chooses the point (4, 10). We check that this is inside Albert’s budget line, on the boldfaced part of Betty’s budget line. We plot that point in the second panel, where it is labeled B.
Now we can see that Albert’s indifference curve must cross Betty’s. Therefore, they cannot have identical tastes.

slides.text: Now Betty chooses a new B instead, which Albert cannot afford

Difference in taste
---
Do Albert and Betty have identical tastes? 
We certainly have no way to rule out that possibility. 
If these indifference curves are extended indefinitely in either direction, they might eventually cross—or they might not.

Difference in taste
---
What about the real world? 
We can replace Albert and Betty with “the average German” and “the average Italian”
We can use realistic numbers for the prices of tomatoes and potatoes.

Difference in taste
---
Then we can repeat the exercise with Germans and Greeks, or Greeks and Italians, or Poles and Hungarians, and with more than just two goods. 
If we ever get a picture like the first one, we’ve spotted a taste difference.

Difference in taste
---
Harvard Professor Hendrik Houthakker (亨德里克·豪特哈克）carried out this exercise for European countries and found no evidence of any taste differences. 
When Houthakker drew his graphs, none looked like the first one
Instead, every one of his pictures look like the second one
This leaves open the possibility that tastes could be either the same or different.
Application 3The Least Bad Tax(or which tax do you prefer?)

The Least Bad Tax
---
Which would you rather pay: 
a percentage wage tax : the government takes a certain percent of your earnings, or 
a head tax : the government takes a certain number of dollars every day, regardless of how much you earn
Suppose that the money collected from you are the same under two types of tax.

Numerical example
---
Suppose you earn 20 an hour. 
The government can impose a 50% wage tax
In this case, you will (optimally choose to) work 10 hours a day, earn 200, and pay 100 in taxes. 
Or the government can impose a 100 daily head tax. 
Which do you prefer?
Budget line: leisure and money

How to formulate this into a consumer choice problem?
---
Begin by drawing your budget line between leisure (measured in hours) and wages (measured in dollars). 
If you don’t work at all, you’ll have 24 hours a day leisure and zero wages, represented by the point (24, 0) 
If you work 24 hours a day, you’ll have zero leisure and $480 in wages, represented by point (0, 480). 
The line connecting these points is your budget line
By choosing the number of hours you work, you can achieve any point on this line.

Head tax
---
Now consider a head tax
The amount collected is still 100
Suppose you still worked for 10 hours 
(notice that this might NOT be optimal for you now, because price changed but you do not reoptimize. In other word, still working for 10 Hours is a lower bound for your welfare under the head tax)

Intuition
---
You might be surprised to learn that one tax can be preferable to another, even when they both collect the same amount of revenue. 
What’s the intuition behind this result?

Intuition: marginal analysis
---
Suppose first that you’re subject to the wage tax, so that your after-tax income is 10 per hour. 
Then, you choose point P 
At this point, the marginal value of your leisure is exactly equal to your 10-per-hour wage rate.
slides.notes:
You might be surprised to learn that one tax can be preferable to another, even
when they both collect the same amount of revenue. But here’s a simpler example:
Which do you prefer, a $0 head tax or a 5,000,000% tax on shoes? Note that both
taxes collect the same amount of revenue: Under the head tax, you pay nothing, and
under the shoe tax, you also pay nothing, because you’ll surely choose to go barefoot.
Nevertheless, it’s better to pay the zero-dollar head tax and buy a pair of shoes.

slides.text:
Intuition: marginal analysis
---
Now if the wage tax is suddenly abandoned and replaced by a head tax, you have the opportunity to earn 20 for an additional hour of work. 
Because the marginal value of your leisure is only $10 per hour, you’ll welcome this opportunity and consider yourself better off.

Intuition (2)
---
An extreme example to build intuition:
Which do you prefer, a 0% head tax or a 5,000,000% sales tax on shoes? 
In both case, government collect zero tax revenue, because you’ll surely choose to go barefoot if a pair of shoes cost 1,000,000RMB.
Nevertheless, it’s better to pay the zero-dollar head tax and buy a pair of shoes under the zero head tax.

Demand elasticity
---
We have already learned the law of demand last time. 
Suppose we want more precise answers as to exactly how responsive quantity demanded is to a change in price. 
Widely used by economics: elasticity.

Elasticity
---
Elasticity measures the sensitivity of one economic variable to a change in another. 
It tells us how much one variable changes when another changes. 
More precisely, elasticity is a ratio of percentage changes in variables.

Elasticity
---
Note that elasticity is NOT the same as the slope of a line. 
By measuring changes in percentage terms, elasticity goes a step deeper than the slope relationship. 
Elasticity is an important concept because it takes into account not only the direction of change but also the size of the change.

Elasticity
---
Elasticities come in many forms, but in this chapter we focus on the most important ones associated with demand curves. 
1. The price elasticity of demand
2. The cross-price elasticity of demand
3. The income elasticity of demand

The price elasticity of demand
---
Two features of this computation are important.

The price elasticity of demand
---
First, because of the Law of Demand, the price elasticity of demand will generally be negative. 
The negative sign is inconvenient, so we often drop the minus sign when reporting (so we are using the absolute value)
Note that higher price elasticities mean that consumers are more responsive to a change in price.

The price elasticity of demand
---
Second, whether the price elasticity of demand greater than or less than 1
Greater than one: call it elastic
Less than one: call it inelastic
Equal to one: unit elasticity

The price elasticity of demand
---
Extreme case: perfectly elastic and perfectly inelastic
Elasticity is infinite: demand is highly responsive to price changes: the smallest increase in price causes consumers to stop consuming the good altogether. 
Demand can also be perfectly inelastic, which means that quantity demanded is completely unaffected by price.

Jevons' Paradox?
---
Jevons‘ Paradox:  
As technological improvements increase the efficiency of resource, the overall demand for that resource can actually increase rather than decrease.
From basic microeconomics the Jevon’s Paradox is no paradox at all.

Determinants of demand elasticities
---
2. Budget share spent on the good. 
The budget share relates to how important the good
   is in your consumption bundle. 
If It is just not important to your overall budget, perhaps you will not be sensitive to price changes, even large ones.
 As you spend more of your budget on a good, the price elasticity of demand should increase
slides.notes:
The budget share relates to how important the good is in your consumption bundle.  
People should give more weight to “important” goods and less weight to unimportant ones. 
If the good represents a small fraction of your overall purchases, you will not be overly concerned if the price increases.  
It is just not important to your overall budget and so you are not sensitive to price changes, even large ones. 
Alternatively, if the good represents a large fraction of your budget—say, a house  or furniture purchase—then you are likely to be more responsive to price changes.

slides.text:

---
3. Available time to adjust. 
When the price of oil jumps to a high level, would everyone immediately stop driving? 
Of course not.
What happens when the price stay high for a longer time period?
slides.notes:
Time is an important element in that people are more
responsive to price changes in the long run than in the short run.

slides.text: The Cross-Price Elasticity

Complements v.s. Substitutes
---
If a cross-price elasticity is negative, then we say the two goods are complements. 
The fall in the price of one leads to a right shift in the demand curve for another. 
Example: Macbook and iPhone

Complements v.s. Substitutes
---
If a cross-price elasticity is positive, then we say the two goods are substitutes. 
Example: iPhone and Huawei Phone
The Income Elasticity of Demand

Normal vs inferior goods
---
Normal goods: when income rises, consumers buy more of that good. Income elas.>0
Inferior goods: when income rises, consumers buy less of that good. Income elas.<0
